label: input token l during the original phase
explanation: A token detector for the letter l while the original sequence is being read. It fires on every original-phase step whose input is l (dev precision 1.0, recall 0.99), at any position and for any L, and also on repeated l occurrences. Activation is fairly uniform (median 0.63 of max 0.85). The strongest examples tend to be an l at the last original position, just before <DEL>, but this was only seen in examples and not checked systematically. It does not fire on the delimiter step. It barely fires in the copy phase, even when l is fed back as an input: there are only weak traces (about 0.13 of max) on copy-phase l inputs and on some original-phase i inputs, which together hold 0.2% of the activation mass.

issues: On the test split the predicate scores precision 1.0, recall 0.990, F1 0.995 and mass recall 0.998, with 0 false positives. Every miss is low-magnitude: coverage of the lowest activation quartile is 0.96, and the other three quartiles are 1.0.

The 1063 test misses are weak traces of about 0.12-0.18 of max. They come in two groups. Some are original-phase i inputs: the predicate (phase==0)&(in_tok==i) has precision 0.006, so i alone does not drive the feature. Others are copy-phase l inputs: (phase==2)&(in_tok==l) has precision 0.005. Together these hold 0.2% of the activation mass, matching the explanation. This is scattered noise, not a systematic class.

Magnitude is modulated by context, and the explanation only partly notes this. The top examples are an l at the last original position, often in sequences that begin with u/t/n. But (phase==0)&(l)&(to_go==0) covers only 15% recall at precision 1, and activation mass is roughly uniform across to_go. So this is a magnitude effect, not a gap in the predicate, and the explanation correctly says it was not checked systematically.
The delimiter step has 0 activations, and the copy phase holds 0.001 of the mass. Both are consistent with the claims.
